name: New Confucianism
summary: New Confucianism (Modern Confucianism) is a twentieth-century Chinese philosophical movement, centred on Xiong Shili's followers Mou Zongsan, Tang Junyi and Xu Fuguan and their 1958 Manifesto on Chinese culture, that defends Confucian moral metaphysics against wholesale Westernization and Marxism. It holds that Chinese culture must develop science and democratic constitutional government out of its own moral foundations: every person is an equal moral and political subject, so monarchy and one-party dictatorship are rejected and power should change hands through free elections under a constitution. It condemns communism as a denial of universal human nature and freedom, criticizes imperialism and the spiritual emptiness of modern Western culture, and upholds filial piety, cultural continuity and a non-dogmatic Confucian religiosity tolerant of all faiths.
scope: As the defining scholarship sets it out: the SEP entry on Modern Confucianism (s1) says New Confucianism 'specifically usually refers to' Xiong Shili's followers Mou Zongsan, Tang Junyi and Xu Fuguan and their followers, and names their 1958 'New Confucian Manifesto' (co-signed with Zhang Junmai) as the movement's watershed; Sernelj (s2, s9) and the IEP entry on Mou (s4) describe the same second-generation group. The profile is answered from the Manifesto's Chinese text (s7), the SEP and IEP entries, Sernelj's studies of the Manifesto and of Xu Fuguan, and Fröhlich's study of Tang Junyi (s8). Where the three thinkers differ, the answer says so. Jiang Qing's mainland 'political Confucianism' and Confucian meritocracy are excluded: the SEP presents Confucian meritocracy as a later anti-democratic view the New Confucians 'would have rejected'. Classical Confucianism and Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism are other subjects. The movement never governed, so it has no record of its own and every answer rests on its words.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Tang held that China's modernization requires a civil society organized by law, contract and the division of industrial labour.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The manifesto criticizes monarchic absolutism; Jiang Qing's hereditary house is a minority view.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Technology valued but subordinate to moral wisdom.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Tang situated Confucian religiosity within a liberal constitution guaranteeing religious freedom and made tolerance of every religion its central civic task.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Third-generation figures accept an adaptation to modern capitalism; the manifesto does not predict collapse.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The Manifesto ties imperialism and colonial wars to industrial expansion, and Tang saw economic interests pushing states into imperialist politics, but both trace the root to Western culture or to the state's weakness and deny it is inevitable.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The manifesto grants Western progress universal value but criticizes capitalism's antagonisms; split.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Tang held that politics must not judge the contents of humanistic culture and condemned the communist subordination of the arts and sciences to political standards.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Tang held that the Confucian tradition is not to be preserved in its entirety, that inherited customs must pass the test of each person's moral judgement rather than be accepted blindly, and that citizens should debate which traditions to follow.

character-from-environment.rationale: Mou and Tang posit innate moral nature, the moral heart-mind.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Manifesto counts the antagonism of labour and capital among the problems modern Western culture produced, welcomes the measures Western states took against it, and rejects the Marxist account of human nature as class nature.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The manifesto rejects Marxist-Leninism and the communist ideology as anti-human and dogmatic.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Manifesto makes every person an equal political subject in a democratic constitutional state, and Tang explicitly rejected a Confucian theocracy and any clerical structure leading to a state religion.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The manifesto says Chinese culture values competition less than the West and offers moral compassion as a corrective.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Manifesto says the constitution should be made 'according to the common will of every person', that all hold equal political rights, and that power must pass peacefully through free elections under a constitution all observe.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The manifesto points to spiritual emptiness and alienation of modernity and capitalism.

culture-before-state.rationale: The Manifesto holds that Chinese culture's moral spirit must be renewed and that democratic state forms must grow from it.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The Manifesto says ancient Chinese culture was of higher objective value than that of the surrounding peoples and that Western science and democracy have universal value, though China and the West should now regard each other as equals.

defeat-communism.rationale: The manifesto and Mou strongly opposed communism and predicted the regime's fall; policy of confrontation not explicit.

democracy-best.rationale: The Manifesto calls democratic constitutional government the only way out of China's cycle of order and chaos and a requirement of Confucian moral spirit itself; Tang held democracy imperfect but better than any alternative at realizing reason.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The manifesto condemns communist dictatorship as anti-human and anti-democratic.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Manifesto reads the old 'mandate of Heaven' as the people's will and grounds modern authority in a constitution made by the common will of all; Tang notes the modern state no longer represents Heaven's order.

dominated-front.rationale: The Manifesto warns that Asian and African nationalism joined with communism against the West serves Soviet ambitions, and says these peoples should instead join with the free and democratic culture of the West.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The Manifesto blames hereditary succession for China's dynastic cycle of disorder and rejects any office that can be held but not given up, asking that power pass by free elections instead.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Manifesto says the only way to avoid bloody succession struggles is for the whole people to hold free elections under a common constitution, so that political power changes hands peacefully.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The Manifesto counts the League of Nations and the UN among the West's answers to narrow nationalism, but Tang later said the UN had lost its authentic value and that concentrating coercive power even in a global body would not bring peace.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Manifesto grounds democracy in the Confucian 'equality of personhood' and the belief that everyone can become a sage, and affirms equal political rights for all; Tang founds the highest dignity of every person on the moral heart-mind all possess.

filial-duty.rationale: Tang held filiality rests on moral reason with absolute significance, even if parents do not love the child.

freedom-is-self-government-of-desire.rationale: Tang defined freedom as moral and spiritual self-fulfilment, the building of one's own character, and the movement holds that the moral heart-mind stands above and apart from desire.

gradual-change.rationale: They sought development of democracy from within tradition rather than rupture, and criticized communism and May Fourth iconoclasm.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The Manifesto counts the industrial revolution among Western achievements of universal and lasting value and calls for China's own industrialization.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The Manifesto says every country not yet democratic must take the road of democratic nation-building and that China's own culture requires democracy, while insisting that democracy be grown from Chinese roots rather than imported as a foreign product.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Tang held that Confucian religiosity has no catechism or revealed scripture and must not compete with constitutional guarantees or dominate the constitutional order, and the Manifesto wants laws made under a constitution set by the common will.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The manifesto rejects Marxist-Leninist materialism; the movement holds moral mind and culture are foundational.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Manifesto finds a 'fundamental contradiction' between Confucian moral spirit and monarchy, says even a sage-king leaves the people's moral subjecthood unrealized, and concludes Chinese politics must abolish the monarchy for democracy.

more-religion-public.rationale: Tang hoped for a renaissance of the Confucian religious spirit as a civil religion supporting civic virtue in a future democracy, but wanted it to spread through society by example, not through the state or organisations.

national-church-status.rationale: Tang rejected a Confucian state religion and theocracy and held that no humanistic tradition, Confucianism included, should receive political protection above all others.

national-rebirth.rationale: The manifesto calls for reconstruction of Chinese culture, though as cultural renewal not radical politics.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Manifesto endorses the independence of all colonies and asks the West, in the Confucian spirit of restoring extinguished states, to help every people complete its own democratic nation-building.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The manifesto criticizes both Western capitalism's problems and communism, but the third generation accommodates capitalism.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Xu held that the government's first duty is to provide for the people's material needs, and Tang that the state must safeguard their freedom, safety and livelihood and the conditions for their ethical life.

one-party-rule.rationale: The manifesto rejects the communist one-party dictatorship as anti-democratic and criticizes the Nationalists' use of tradition to justify one-party rule.

organic-representation.rationale: The Manifesto asks that political power become transferable peacefully between political parties under a constitution, and Tang wanted parties without ideology rather than no parties.

party-controls-media.rationale: Rejected as part of communist totalitarianism; manifesto defends free evolution of humanity.

person-over-state.rationale: Mou, Tang and the 1958 Manifesto ground democracy in the moral dignity of the person, so the state serves persons, though they also stress duty to the community.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rule by personal loyalty is incompatible with the democratic constitutionalism they advocate.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Tang relieved politics of claims to a higher moral truth, describing it as the contest of wills and the procedures that temper it, and warned that bringing absolute truth into politics leads to totalitarianism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The thinkers are described as cultural nationalists who defended Chinese culture and wanted modernization to realize its ideals.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: The Manifesto asks the West, as the leading power of the world, to help 'complete every people's demand for democratic nation-building', and says every country not yet democratic must take that road.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The manifesto calls for democratic constitutionality and law to replace rule by rulers' whim.

property-franchise.rationale: The Manifesto calls for affirming equal political rights for every person and making public office open to all as equal political subjects.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Tang rejected Confucian theocracy and wanted Confucianism to be a meeting place for all religions within a constitution guaranteeing religious freedom; the Manifesto praises Confucianism for having no hell for heretics.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Manifesto affirms that every person has equal political rights and that public office must be open to everyone as an equal political subject.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Tang called moral-mind belief a faith or postulate, and held religious belief in an absolute spiritual reality is essential.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Modern Confucians reinterpret the tradition for modernity, as Mou reinterpreted Kant and tradition into moral metaphysics.

religion-illusion.rationale: Tang held religious belief in an absolute spiritual reality is essential, and the manifesto rejects Marxist materialism.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Tang held that different religions are different ways of attaining sagehood whose ultimate destination may be the same, and the Manifesto says the sages of every place share the same mind and principle.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The tradition reserves a right of the people to judge rulers (Mencius) and the manifesto supports constitutional limits on rulers.

restore-past-order.rationale: They want to renew tradition while adopting democracy and science, not return to the old imperial order.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Tang assumed a liberal constitution guaranteeing religious freedom and stressed each person's 'absolute' freedom to choose their own ideals.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Manifesto grants that the communist dictatorship may achieve some collective technical results for a time, yet says it must not last because it violates individual freedom and human rights, and it rejected the Nationalists' long 'tutelage' too.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Tang held that parties in a democracy need no ideology or philosophy, only practical strategies, and that politicians should deal with concrete issues rather than rely on abstract principles, which lead to totalitarianism.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to affirmation of civilization, science and culture.

rule-by-example.rationale: Mou argued that the traditional reliance on a virtuous ruler failed and that objective democratic institutions must carry political virtue; Xu, though keeping rule by virtue as an ideal, held it is realized only when democracy binds rulers whether or not they are virtuous.

sacred-nation.rationale: Tang held the state's ethical life worthy of religious reverence and the Manifesto speaks of the nation's objective spiritual life lasting for ages, though Tang insisted on cosmopolitan patriotism over nationalism.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Tang held that modern Confucianism abandons the idea of an immediate presence of absolute truth in politics as embodied in the imperial Son of Heaven, and the Manifesto rejects the old maxim 'the Heavenly King is sage and wise'.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: They defend cultural heritage; the May Fourth iconoclasm and communist treatment of tradition are the criticized foils.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The defining thinkers place morality in a heart-mind above desire and reject utilitarianism, though Tang's modern Confucianism no longer condemns the pursuit of self-interest in civil society.

separate-church-state.rationale: Tang placed Confucian religiosity outside the state: under a constitution guaranteeing religious freedom it must not seek to dominate the state, the state stays neutral towards citizens' religions, and no tradition, Confucianism included, gets political protection above others.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Mou's moral metaphysics holds all humans share a moral nature grounding dignity and rights, a central claim of the mainstream.

single-common-good.rationale: Xu wanted the common interest based on shared morality rather than individual interests checking each other, but Tang relieved politics of claims to a higher moral truth and saw it as a contest of wills settled by procedures; the defining thinkers point both ways.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Rulers abusing power is condemned and constitutionality urged.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The 1958 Manifesto and Mou's moral metaphysics hold that human nature is moral and spiritual and that politics must be grounded in it.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Tang strongly rejected Marx's account of the state as a relation of class rule, holding that the state is the objectification of human reason.

state-harmful.rationale: The tradition treats government as a moral institution, and Mou's project of a new 'outer kingship' through democracy presupposes a state.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Communist anti-religion rejected; Tang said religious belief essential.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Tang wanted the state to secure the conditions for ethical life yet held that politics must not judge the contents of culture or protect any tradition above others; Xu's rule by 'non-action' means rulers do not impose their preferences.

strong-leader.rationale: The manifesto calls for democratic constitutionality to end monarchic absolutism, rejecting unchecked rulers.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The manifesto says China needs science and technology but warns that Western progress produced severe problems and that moral wisdom is primary.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The 1958 Manifesto argues for accepting science and democracy while renewing Chinese moral culture, which is exactly this combination.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Manifesto calls destroying another people's state and its ancestral sacrifices unjust in Confucian thought and condemns Western imperialism, colonial conquest and wars for colonies.

total-state.rationale: The manifesto condemns totalitarianism as in the Soviet case.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Tang grouped Italian Fascism, National Socialism, Stalinism and Chinese communism together under totalitarianism, and the Manifesto blames both communist and fascist influences for China's failed democracy.

traditional-family.rationale: Tang held filiality has absolute significance, grounded in moral reason, and the family is central to Confucian ethics.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The Manifesto presents Chinese culture as a living continuity from antiquity and calls for its preservation and renewal.

universal-morality.rationale: Mou argued intellectual intuition is available to all and moral value is objective; Tang held the moral heart-mind is universal.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Mou's inner sage and outer king ideal requires moral cultivation to be joined with public engagement.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Manifesto holds that every person is equally a political subject with equal political rights and that public offices should be open to everyone.

missingStatements.text: Government officials should be chosen for moral character and cultivated virtue.
missingStatements.rationale: Mou, Xu and Tang treat politics as grounded in moral mind and Jiang Qing's chambers rest on virtue-based legitimacy; moral-cultivation leadership is central.

missingStatements.text: Democratic institutions are needed but must be grounded in a shared moral vision of the person rather than treated as morally neutral procedures.
missingStatements.rationale: Mou held democracy is not itself a moral system yet requires moral foundations, and Tang held democracy needs a vision of persons as moral beings while rejecting purely political liberalism.
missingStatements.declined: Compound claim about democracy's moral grounding; democracy-best and single-common-good cover what other ideologies can answer.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-09), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-19) leaned on Wikipedia (s3, s5, s6) and treated Jiang Qing's political Confucianism as a dissenting branch; the SEP (s1) instead sets Confucian meritocracy apart from New Confucianism, so answers resting on Jiang Qing were nulled, and every other first-pass answer was checked against the sources and kept, changed or nulled, with the first version kept in each statement's reviewHistory. This pass read in full the Manifesto (s7, Chinese text), the SEP and IEP entries, Sernelj's chapter and article, and the political chapters of Fröhlich's study of Tang (chs. 1, 8-10, 12). Themes searched: government and democracy (Manifesto sections 9-10, SEP section 5, Fröhlich ch. 9), religion (Manifesto section 5, Fröhlich ch. 10), society and family (Manifesto section 7, Fröhlich ch. 8), world and imperialism (Manifesto section 11, Fröhlich ch. 8), economy (all sources). The movement's thinkers wrote little on economic policy: Fröhlich notes Tang never discussed capitalism or market economics, and Xu Fuguan's socialist sympathies and wish for land reform (s9) date from his political career before he became a Confucian scholar, so economic, ecological, technological and most world-policy statements stay null. Mou's and Xu's own political essays (e.g. Mou's Authority and Governance) were not available online in a citable copy.
